The 1990s, one event per year.German reunification: East and West Germany were reunited on October 3, 1990, less than a year after the Berlin Wall fell. The date is now a national holiday.
The 1990s, one event per year.USSR dissolves: Mikhail Gorbachev resigned on Christmas Day 1991, and 15 republics became independent countries.
The 1990s, one event per year.Maastricht Treaty signed: The treaty created the European Union and set the economic rules that countries needed to meet to join the euro.
The 1990s, one event per year.Oslo Accords: Rabin and Arafat shook hands on the White House lawn. The deal itself had been secretly negotiated in Norway.
The 1990s, one event per year.Mandela becomes president: After his first all-race election, Mandela became president, having spent 27 years in prison.
The 1990s, one event per year.Srebrenica massacre: Over 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed in July. Courts have ruled it genocide.
The 1990s, one event per year.Taliban take Kabul: The Taliban took the Afghan capital in September 1996 and ruled most of Afghanistan until 2001.
The 1990s, one event per year.Hong Kong handover: On July 1, Britain returned its colony to China under a 'one country, two systems' formula.
The 1990s, one event per year.Good Friday Agreement: The deal, also known as the Belfast Agreement, was approved by voters on both sides of the Irish border and brought most of the Troubles to an end.
The 1990s, one event per year.Euro launched: The euro began on January 1, 1999 as an accounting currency. Cash notes and coins arrived only in 2002.

When these adopted the Gregorian calenda.Spain: The pope's reform skipped ten days in October 1582, so 4 October was followed by 15 October.
When these adopted the Gregorian calenda.Duchy of Prussia: Protestant territories long distrusted a Catholic pope's calendar, so adoption here lagged decades behind Catholic lands.
When these adopted the Gregorian calenda.Protestant German states: These states skipped 11 days, from 18 February to 1 March, ending a century of confusion between Protestant and Catholic dates.
When these adopted the Gregorian calenda.Britain and its colonies: Eleven days vanished, and the British tax year still starts April 6, the old April 5 shifted for the missing days.
When these adopted the Gregorian calenda.Alaska: The switch came with the US purchase and also moved it across the date line, giving it two Fridays in a row.
When these adopted the Gregorian calenda.Japan: Japan leapt from 2 December 1872 straight to 1 January 1873, replacing a lunisolar calendar.
When these adopted the Gregorian calenda.China: The new republic adopted it at its founding, though warlords and the public kept using old dates for decades.
When these adopted the Gregorian calenda.Russia: The Bolsheviks decreed it, so 31 January was followed by 14 February and the October Revolution is dated in November.
When these adopted the Gregorian calenda.Greece: It was the last European country to adopt it, after the Orthodox church had resisted for centuries.
When these adopted the Gregorian calenda.Turkey: Atatürk's reforms put Turkey on this calendar in 1926, two years before the switch to the Latin alphabet.

Novels, by when their story is set.The Name of the Rose: Umberto Eco's medieval murder mystery is set in an Italian abbey; Sean Connery played the detective monk in the film.
Novels, by when their story is set.Wolf Hall: Hilary Mantel's novel follows Thomas Cromwell and won the Booker Prize in 2009.
Novels, by when their story is set.The Three Musketeers: Dumas's novel unfolds under Louis XIII; d'Artagnan was based on a real musketeer.
Novels, by when their story is set.The Scarlet Letter: Hawthorne added the 'w' to his name to distance himself from an ancestor who judged the Salem witch trials.
Novels, by when their story is set.The Last of the Mohicans: Set during the French and Indian War, it features the siege of Fort William Henry.
Novels, by when their story is set.A Tale of Two Cities: Dickens's story opens 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times'.
Novels, by when their story is set.War and Peace: Tolstoy's novel follows Napoleon's invasion of Russia and has around 580 characters.
Novels, by when their story is set.Les Misérables: Hugo's novel climaxes in the June Rebellion of 1832, with barricades in Paris.
Novels, by when their story is set.Gone with the Wind: Margaret Mitchell's only novel in her lifetime won a Pulitzer Prize in 1937.
Novels, by when their story is set.The Great Gatsby: Fitzgerald's novel of the Jazz Age sold poorly in his lifetime.

Ways to say hello, by first appearance.The first postage stamp: The Penny Black, issued in Britain in 1840, bore Queen Victoria's portrait and made the sender, not the receiver, pay.
Ways to say hello, by first appearance.The first Christmas card: Henry Cole commissioned it in 1843; one design showed a family drinking wine, which drew criticism.
Ways to say hello, by first appearance.Morse's first telegram: What hath God wrought was sent from Washington to Baltimore on 24 May 1844.
Ways to say hello, by first appearance.The telephone: Alexander Graham Bell patented it in 1876, and his first words were reportedly Mr. Watson, come here.
Ways to say hello, by first appearance.Commercial radio broadcast: KDKA in Pittsburgh began broadcasting in November 1920 with presidential election returns.
Ways to say hello, by first appearance.Email: Ray Tomlinson sent the first network email in 1971 and chose the @ sign for addresses.
Ways to say hello, by first appearance.Handheld mobile phone call: Martin Cooper of Motorola called a rival at Bell Labs on 3 April 1973 from a handset weighing about a kilogram.
Ways to say hello, by first appearance.SMS text message: The first text, Merry Christmas, was sent in December 1992 to a Vodafone director.
Ways to say hello, by first appearance.Emoji (in Japan): Shigetaka Kurita created 176 emoji for NTT DoCoMo in 1999, and they are now in the MoMA collection.
Ways to say hello, by first appearance.The iPhone: Steve Jobs announced it in January 2007 as an iPod, a phone and an internet communicator in one.

Kings of England, by when they took the.Alfred the Great: Alfred the Great defended Wessex against Viking invaders, and he is the only English monarch called the Great.
Kings of England, by when they took the.Æthelred the Unready: Æthelred the Unready's nickname actually means ill-advised, and it came from a pun on his name, which meant noble counsel.
Kings of England, by when they took the.Cnut: Cnut ruled England, Denmark and Norway, and legend has it he sat on the beach to show that even a king cannot hold back the tide.
Kings of England, by when they took the.Edward the Confessor: Edward the Confessor founded Westminster Abbey, and he was known for his piety, and he died without an heir, setting up the events of 1066.
Kings of England, by when they took the.William the Conqueror: William the Conqueror's Domesday Book recorded England's lands and property, and the survey was completed in about a year.
Kings of England, by when they took the.Henry II: Henry II was the husband of Eleanor of Aquitaine, and he reigned over a huge Angevin empire, and his quarrel with Becket ended in murder.
Kings of England, by when they took the.Richard the Lionheart: Richard the Lionheart spent only a few months of his reign in England, and he was famous as a crusader.
Kings of England, by when they took the.Edward Longshanks: Edward Longshanks was nicknamed for his height, and he was known as the Hammer of the Scots.
Kings of England, by when they took the.Henry V: Henry V won a stunning victory at Agincourt, and Shakespeare wrote a play about him that includes the speech about a band of brothers.
Kings of England, by when they took the.Richard III: Richard III was killed at Bosworth, and his skeleton was found beneath a car park in Leicester in 2012.

Count the legs.Snake: Boas and pythons keep tiny pelvic spurs, remnants of the legs that their ancestors had.
Count the legs.Penguin: Their legs are short but stout, and a huddling emperor penguin balances its egg on its feet.
Count the legs.Kangaroo: Kangaroos cannot walk backwards, and they use the tail as a fifth leg when moving slowly.
Count the legs.Ladybug: Their bright colour warns predators of bitter-tasting chemicals in their blood.
Count the legs.Scorpion: They glow under ultraviolet light, and they have eight legs plus a pair of pincers.
Count the legs.Crab: Crabs belong to the decapods, which means ten-footed, and the front pair carry the claws.
Count the legs.Woodlouse: These are crustaceans, not insects, and they breathe through gill-like structures.
Count the legs.Caterpillar (incl. prolegs): They have six true legs plus fleshy prolegs, and the true legs become the butterfly's.
Count the legs.House centipede: They have 30 legs and chase down insects with surprising speed.
Count the legs.Illacme plenipes millipede: This California millipede has more legs than any other known animal, up to 750.

Happy accidents: when they were discover.Potato chips (legend): According to legend, chef George Crum made the first potato chips in 1853 for a customer who complained that his fries were too thick.
Happy accidents: when they were discover.Saccharin: Saccharin was found when Constantin Fahlberg noticed that his hands tasted sweet, after forgetting to wash them following lab work.
Happy accidents: when they were discover.Corn flakes: John Harvey Kellogg and his brother Will found by accident that stale wheat dough rolled into flakes, and invented flaked cereal.
Happy accidents: when they were discover.Popsicle: Eleven-year-old Frank Epperson reportedly left soda and a stirring stick outside on a freezing night, and invented the popsicle.
Happy accidents: when they were discover.Penicillin: Alexander Fleming noticed that mold on a forgotten petri dish had killed the bacteria around it, and found penicillin.
Happy accidents: when they were discover.Teflon: Roy Plunkett, a DuPont chemist, found a frozen container of gas that had turned into a slippery white solid, which became Teflon.
Happy accidents: when they were discover.Super Glue: Harry Coover was trying to make clear plastic gun sights when he found a compound that stuck to everything, and later it was sold as Super Glue.
Happy accidents: when they were discover.Microwave oven: Percy Spencer noticed that a candy bar in his pocket melted near a radar device, which led to the microwave oven.
Happy accidents: when they were discover.Play-Doh (as a toy): Play-Doh began life as a wallpaper cleaner, until a teacher noticed that kids enjoyed molding it, and it was relaunched as a toy.
Happy accidents: when they were discover.Post-it Note glue: Spencer Silver was trying to create a strong adhesive and made a weak, reusable one instead, and it later became the sticky part of Post-its.

Deep-sky favorites by Messier number.Crab Nebula: Charles Messier listed it first in 1758 as a fixed fuzzy object that wasn't a comet. It is the remnant of a supernova seen from Earth in 1054.
Deep-sky favorites by Messier number.Hercules Globular Cluster: The northern sky's brightest globular cluster holds several hundred thousand stars. In 1974 the Arecibo radio message was beamed toward it.
Deep-sky favorites by Messier number.Andromeda Galaxy: The nearest large galaxy to the Milky Way, about 2.5 million light-years away, visible to the naked eye in dark skies. It will merge with ours in billions of years.
Deep-sky favorites by Messier number.Orion Nebula: A glowing stellar nursery visible to the naked eye in Orion's sword, about 1,300 light-years away, where new stars are forming now.
Deep-sky favorites by Messier number.The Pleiades: The "Seven Sisters" star cluster is visible with the naked eye and is known across many cultures, including Japan, where it's called Subaru.
Deep-sky favorites by Messier number.Whirlpool Galaxy: The first galaxy recognized as having spiral structure, found by Lord Rosse in 1845 using a giant telescope in Ireland.
Deep-sky favorites by Messier number.Ring Nebula: A ring-shaped planetary nebula in Lyra, the dying remains of a Sun-like star, visible even in small telescopes as a smoke ring.
Deep-sky favorites by Messier number.Bode's Galaxy: A spiral galaxy in Ursa Major, about 12 million light-years away, which pairs with the "Cigar Galaxy" nearby, M82.
Deep-sky favorites by Messier number.Virgo A galaxy: A giant elliptical galaxy in Virgo, whose central black hole was the first ever photographed, by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2019.
Deep-sky favorites by Messier number.Sombrero Galaxy: A galaxy named for the broad-brimmed hat shape its bright bulge and dark dust lane make, about 29 million light-years away. Messier's own list ended at M103.

Tyre speed rating letters.N: The slowest rating here at 140 km/h, rarely seen on cars. The sequence isn't alphabetical, which is the great quirk of tyre ratings.
Tyre speed rating letters.Q: Rated for 160 km/h, it is a common rating on studded and winter tyres, which put grip ahead of speed.
Tyre speed rating letters.R: Rated 170 km/h, it is typically found on heavy-duty light-truck and van tyres, where load capacity matters more than speed.
Tyre speed rating letters.S: Rated 180 km/h, it is a standard rating for many family sedans and vans, enough for any legal limit.
Tyre speed rating letters.T: Rated 190 km/h, it is common on all-season tyres for everyday family cars.
Tyre speed rating letters.U: Rated 200 km/h, well above the legal limit in nearly every country. A rating shows what the tyre can safely withstand, not permission to drive that fast.
Tyre speed rating letters.H: The odd letter: H sits between U and V, rather than in alphabetical order, because it was in use before the later letters were added around it.
Tyre speed rating letters.V: Rated 240 km/h, common on sports sedans and coupes. A higher rating usually means a stiffer sidewall and sharper handling.
Tyre speed rating letters.W: Rated 270 km/h. Tyres at this level are made for supercars and performance sedans, built to resist heat build-up at high speeds.
Tyre speed rating letters.Y: The highest rating here at 300 km/h, fitted to the fastest road cars. A tyre this fast must survive huge centrifugal force and heat.

Still going! When these began.Oxford Electric Bell: It rings so softly you can barely hear it, in Oxford's Clarendon Laboratory.
Still going! When these began.Broadbalk wheat experiment: At Rothamsted in England, it is the oldest continuous agricultural experiment.
Still going! When these began.Beal's buried seed experiment: William Beal buried bottles of seeds at Michigan State, to dig up and test germination over many decades.
Still going! When these began.Centennial Light bulb: It's a hand-blown bulb in a California fire station, which has burned almost nonstop since 1901.
Still going! When these began.Pitch drop experiment: The ninth drop fell in 2014, and in all this time nobody has ever seen a drop fall.
Still going! When these began.Framingham Heart Study: It helped identify cholesterol and high blood pressure as heart disease risk factors, and coined the term 'risk factor'.
Still going! When these began.The Mousetrap (play): Agatha Christie's play has run in London's West End, and audiences are asked not to reveal the ending.
Still going! When these began.Coronation Street: Set in Weatherfield, it is among the world's longest-running TV soaps.
Still going! When these began.The Simpsons (TV series): It started as shorts on The Tracey Ullman Show before becoming the longest-running American animated sitcom.
Still going! When these began.As Slow As Possible (organ): John Cage's piece in Halberstadt, Germany, is scheduled to last 639 years, ending in 2640.

How many fans these stadiums hold.Fenway Park: Opened in 1912, it is the oldest major league ballpark still in use, famous for its tall Green Monster wall in left field.
How many fans these stadiums hold.Yankee Stadium: The current stadium opened in 2009 across the street from the original House That Ruth Built.
How many fans these stadiums hold.Emirates Stadium: Arsenal moved here in 2006 from Highbury, and the club's nickname the Gunners comes from its origins at an armaments factory.
How many fans these stadiums hold.Old Trafford: Manchester United's home is nicknamed the Theatre of Dreams, and it is the largest club ground in the Premier League.
How many fans these stadiums hold.Maracanã, Rio: In 1950 it hosted the World Cup decider before a crowd estimated near 200,000, the largest ever for a football match.
How many fans these stadiums hold.Signal Iduna Park, Dortmund: Its Yellow Wall is Europe's largest standing terrace, packing about 25,000 Dortmund fans into one stand.
How many fans these stadiums hold.Wembley Stadium: Its steel arch rises about 133 m over the rebuilt stadium, finished in 2007, and it is England's national ground.
How many fans these stadiums hold.Melbourne Cricket Ground: It hosted the 1956 Olympics and is the site of cricket's Boxing Day Test, with Australian rules football in winter.
How many fans these stadiums hold.Michigan Stadium: Nicknamed the Big House, it is the largest stadium in the United States and one of the largest in the world.
How many fans these stadiums hold.Narendra Modi Stadium: In Ahmedabad, it is the world's largest cricket stadium and was renamed in 2021 for India's prime minister.

Grams of sugar in each of these.One strawberry: Strawberries are among the lowest-sugar fruits, and the seeds on the outside are really the fruits, with the red flesh a swollen stalk.
Grams of sugar in each of these.Tablespoon of ketchup: Ketchup began as a Chinese fish sauce called kê-tsiap, and sugar was only added to it much later.
Grams of sugar in each of these.Krispy Kreme glazed doughnut: Krispy Kreme began in 1937 in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, when Vernon Rudolph bought a secret yeast doughnut recipe.
Grams of sugar in each of these.Medium banana: Botanically, a banana is a berry, while a strawberry is not, which makes a banana the more correct berry.
Grams of sugar in each of these.Medium apple: About a quarter of an apple is air, which is why apples float, and why bobbing for them is possible.
Grams of sugar in each of these.Snickers bar (52 g): The bar was named after the Mars family's favourite horse, Snickers, rather than any kind of nut.
Grams of sugar in each of these.Coca-Cola (12 oz can): Pharmacist John Pemberton invented the drink in Atlanta in 1886, and early versions contained extracts of the coca leaf.
Grams of sugar in each of these.Coca-Cola (20 oz bottle): That bottle holds roughly 16 teaspoons of sugar, far more than most health guidelines recommend for an entire day.
Grams of sugar in each of these.Cup of granulated sugar: Table sugar is the chemical sucrose, extracted from sugar cane or sugar beet, and the two sources are indistinguishable once refined.
Grams of sugar in each of these.Cup of honey: Honey is famously long-lasting; pots found in ancient Egyptian tombs are still edible thanks to its low water content.

When these grand hotels opened.Raffles, Singapore: Named for Sir Stamford Raffles, founder of modern Singapore. The Singapore Sling cocktail was invented in its Long Bar around 1915.
When these grand hotels opened.The Savoy, London: Built with profits from Gilbert and Sullivan operas, it was among the first British buildings with electric lighting and electric lifts.
When these grand hotels opened.Château Frontenac, Quebec: A Canadian Pacific Railway hotel crowning Quebec City's skyline, often called the most photographed hotel in the world.
When these grand hotels opened.Ritz Paris: César Ritz's hotel was Coco Chanel's home for decades, and it was where Diana, Princess of Wales, dined before her final car journey.
When these grand hotels opened.The Plaza, New York: Home of the fictional Eloise, and the Beatles stayed here in 1964. It is a New York landmark facing Central Park.
When these grand hotels opened.Beverly Hills Hotel: Nicknamed the Pink Palace, it opened two years before Beverly Hills itself became a city.
When these grand hotels opened.Waldorf Astoria (Park Ave): The Art Deco hotel moved to Park Avenue after the original Fifth Avenue site was demolished to make way for the Empire State Building.
When these grand hotels opened.Burj Al Arab: Built on an artificial island and shaped like a sail. Its 'seven-star' label is a media nickname, not an official rating.
When these grand hotels opened.Atlantis The Palm, Dubai: Sits at the crown of Palm Jumeirah, an artificial palm-shaped island built from reclaimed land.
When these grand hotels opened.Marina Bay Sands: Three towers carry a ship-shaped SkyPark with a huge rooftop infinity pool, about 57 floors above the ground.

Getting around London: when each arrived.Hansom cab patented: Joseph Hansom patented the design in 1834. The two-wheeled cab with its driver perched behind became the symbol of Victorian London.
Getting around London: when each arrived.The Tube opens: The Metropolitan Railway was the world's first underground railway, hauled by steam locomotives from Paddington to Farringdon.
Getting around London: when each arrived.Tower Bridge opens: Its bascules lift to let ships through. It is often mistaken for London Bridge.
Getting around London: when each arrived.Heathrow opens: It started in 1946 as London Airport, on land that had been market gardens and a small airfield.
Getting around London: when each arrived.Routemaster enters service: The classic red double-decker with an open rear platform, designed to be easy to board.
Getting around London: when each arrived.M25 orbital completed: This ring road around Greater London is about 117 miles long, and is one of Europe's busiest motorways.
Getting around London: when each arrived.Eurostar from Waterloo: Trains first ran from Waterloo International, until the service moved to St Pancras in 2007.
Getting around London: when each arrived.London Eye opens: Built for the Millennium, it became the world's tallest cantilevered observation wheel.
Getting around London: when each arrived.Thames cable car opens: The Emirates Air Line crosses the Thames between Greenwich Peninsula and the Royal Docks.
Getting around London: when each arrived.Elizabeth line opens: Named for the late Queen, it opened in 2022 after years of delays, linking Reading and Heathrow to east London.

Bathroom inventions, oldest to newest.Flush toilet (Harington): Sir John Harington, Queen Elizabeth I's godson, designed one with a cistern and valve, but it took centuries to catch on.
Bathroom inventions, oldest to newest.Mass-made toothbrush (Addis): William Addis of London is credited with it, using bone handles and boar bristles, and his firm kept making brushes for over two centuries.
Bathroom inventions, oldest to newest.Packaged toilet paper: Joseph Gayetty sold medicated paper in packs in the US, at a time when most people used newspaper, rags or catalog pages.
Bathroom inventions, oldest to newest.Deodorant (Mum): Mum was the first commercial deodorant, invented in Philadelphia, and was a zinc-based cream that you applied by hand.
Bathroom inventions, oldest to newest.Toothpaste in a tube: Dr. Washington Sheffield of Connecticut packed his dental cream into collapsible metal tubes, borrowing the idea from artists' paint tubes.
Bathroom inventions, oldest to newest.Gillette safety razor: King Gillette's disposable blades popularized the business model of selling cheap handles and then many replacement blades.
Bathroom inventions, oldest to newest.Kotex sanitary pad: Developed from cellulose wadding used as bandages in World War I, Kotex was the first widely sold disposable sanitary pad.
Bathroom inventions, oldest to newest.Q-tips cotton swabs: Leo Gerstenzang got the idea from his wife wrapping cotton around toothpicks; the box now warns against putting them in your ears.
Bathroom inventions, oldest to newest.Crest fluoride toothpaste: Crest was the first toothpaste to win the American Dental Association's endorsement for preventing cavities, in 1960.
Bathroom inventions, oldest to newest.Bic disposable razor: Bic already made cheap ballpoint pens and lighters, and applied the same throwaway idea to shaving.

Old EU appliance energy labels.A+++: This top class was added to the scale in 2010 after fridges and freezers kept getting more efficient than the A rating allowed.
Old EU appliance energy labels.A++: A++ arrived around 2003 for fridges, when ordinary A was no longer good enough to separate the best models.
Old EU appliance energy labels.A+: A+ was introduced around 2003 as a step above A, a patch for appliances that outgrew the original scale.
Old EU appliance energy labels.A: A was once the top of the original A to G scale from the 1990s, and machines had to improve beyond it.
Old EU appliance energy labels.B: Labels color-code the letters from green to red, so a B was a shade of green, still better than average.
Old EU appliance energy labels.C: A mid-scale rating, shown in yellow-green, it meant a typical, unremarkable machine for its era.
Old EU appliance energy labels.D: Under the old scale, this letter appeared in orange, signaling an appliance that used a lot more power than the best.
Old EU appliance energy labels.E: Lower classes like this have mostly been phased out in the EU, as minimum efficiency rules ban the worst models.
Old EU appliance energy labels.F: Close to the bottom of the old scale, it marked appliances that guzzled power compared with the best.
Old EU appliance energy labels.G: Shown in red, this last class marked the most power-hungry appliances, and in 2021 the EU reset the labels to a clean A to G scale.

Shakespeare's life, in order.Born in Stratford: His baptism was recorded on 26 April, and 23 April is the traditional birthday, also the date of his death.
Shakespeare's life, in order.Marries Anne Hathaway: He was 18 and she was around eight years older, and the couple's first daughter was born six months after the wedding.
Shakespeare's life, in order.Twins Hamnet and Judith born: Hamnet's name is close to Hamlet, and some scholars think the boy's death later inspired the play.
Shakespeare's life, in order.Mocked as an 'upstart crow': A rival writer, Robert Greene, wrote of an 'upstart crow' in a pamphlet, the first mention of Shakespeare in London.
Shakespeare's life, in order.Son Hamnet dies: Hamnet was only eleven when he was buried, in August.
Shakespeare's life, in order.The Globe opens: The theatre was built partly from timbers of an earlier playhouse, The Theatre, carried across the Thames.
Shakespeare's life, in order.Becomes one of the King's Men: When James I took over the company, it was renamed the King's Men, and Shakespeare was part of it.
Shakespeare's life, in order.The Globe burns down: A cannon fired during Henry VIII set the thatch on fire, and nobody died, and the theatre was rebuilt the next year.
Shakespeare's life, in order.Dies: His gravestone in Stratford carries a curse on anyone who disturbs his bones.
Shakespeare's life, in order.The First Folio is published: His fellow actors collected the plays, and it saved 18 of them, including Macbeth and The Tempest, from being lost.

The Solar System's big moons by diameter.Enceladus: Saturn's icy moon shoots geysers of water ice from its south pole, hinting at a hidden ocean below.
The Solar System's big moons by diameter.Charon: Pluto's largest moon is about half Pluto's size; the pair are tidally locked and orbit a point in space between them.
The Solar System's big moons by diameter.Titania: Uranus's largest moon is named for the fairy queen in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream.
The Solar System's big moons by diameter.Triton: Neptune's big moon orbits backward, which suggests it was captured from the Kuiper belt, and it has nitrogen geysers.
The Solar System's big moons by diameter.Europa: This Jupiter moon likely hides a salty ocean under its icy crust, and NASA's Europa Clipper launched in 2024 to study it.
The Solar System's big moons by diameter.The Moon: The fifth-largest moon in the Solar System, and the only one besides ours that humans have visited.
The Solar System's big moons by diameter.Io: The most volcanically active world we know, with hundreds of volcanoes powered by tidal squeezing from Jupiter.
The Solar System's big moons by diameter.Callisto: Jupiter's heavily cratered moon has one of the oldest surfaces in the Solar System, barely changed in billions of years.
The Solar System's big moons by diameter.Titan: Saturn's moon has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane, and NASA's Dragonfly rotorcraft is bound for it.
The Solar System's big moons by diameter.Ganymede: The largest moon in the Solar System is bigger than Mercury and the only moon known to have its own magnetic field.

German companies, by founding year.Siemens: Founded by Werner von Siemens in Berlin, starting with a pointer telegraph.
German companies, by founding year.Bayer: Its chemists made aspirin in 1899, and it still sells it.
German companies, by founding year.BASF: Short for Badische Anilin und Soda-Fabrik, in Ludwigshafen, it is among the largest chemical firms in the world.
German companies, by founding year.Deutsche Bank: Founded in Berlin to finance foreign trade, with HQ towers in Frankfurt nicknamed Debit and Credit.
German companies, by founding year.Bosch: Robert Bosch began with a workshop in Stuttgart, building ignition magnetos for cars.
German companies, by founding year.Allianz: Founded in Berlin, one of the world's largest insurers is now headquartered in Munich.
German companies, by founding year.Haribo: Hans Riegel of Bonn gave it his initials, and gold bears came in 1922.
German companies, by founding year.Adidas: Adi Dassler's company was born when he and his brother Rudolf split; Rudolf founded Puma.
German companies, by founding year.SAP: Five former IBM engineers founded it in Walldorf; its business software runs many global firms.
German companies, by founding year.Zalando: The Berlin online fashion retailer started out selling flip-flops.

Rocks and minerals by density.Pumice: Frothy volcanic glass full of air pockets, it can float on the sea in rafts for years.
Rocks and minerals by density.Ice: Ice floats because water is unusual: it expands when it freezes, so lakes freeze from the top down.
Rocks and minerals by density.Coal: This is compressed plant matter from ancient swamps, mostly from the Carboniferous period.
Rocks and minerals by density.Sandstone: The 'rose-red city' of Petra in Jordan is carved from it.
Rocks and minerals by density.Granite: Cooled slowly deep underground, it is hard enough that Mount Rushmore was carved from it.
Rocks and minerals by density.Basalt: The most common rock of the ocean floor; its cooled lava also forms the hexagonal columns of Giant's Causeway.
Rocks and minerals by density.Diamond: Diamonds form about 150 km down, and are carried up by rare volcanic eruptions of kimberlite.
Rocks and minerals by density.Magnetite: Strongly magnetic, it is the main mineral in lodestone, the earliest compass.
Rocks and minerals by density.Galena: This lead ore was used in early crystal radios, where a thin wire called a 'cat's whisker' touched it.
Rocks and minerals by density.Native gold: A one-litre bottle of it would weigh over 19 kilograms, and gold is so dense that most panning relies on its weight.

Coffee's journey from farm to cup.Pick ripe cherries: Coffee beans are seeds of a red fruit called the coffee cherry. The best farms pick only the ripe ones by hand.
Coffee's journey from farm to cup.Remove the fruit pulp: The pulp is not wasted. Dried husks become cascara, a tea-like drink popular in some coffee regions.
Coffee's journey from farm to cup.Ferment the beans: Tanks of beans ferment for around 12 to 48 hours to break down sticky mucilage. Too long and they turn sour.
Coffee's journey from farm to cup.Dry the beans: Beans lie on raised beds or patios for around two weeks and are raked often so they dry evenly.
Coffee's journey from farm to cup.Hull off the parchment: The papery parchment layer around each bean is stripped by hulling machines, leaving the pale green bean.
Coffee's journey from farm to cup.Ship the green beans: Green beans keep for months, which is why most roasting happens close to the drinker, not at the farm.
Coffee's journey from farm to cup.Roast: Roasting triggers the Maillard reaction, creating hundreds of aroma compounds. Beans audibly crack as they expand.
Coffee's journey from farm to cup.Grind: Coffee goes stale fast once ground, losing much of its aroma within minutes, so grind just before brewing.
Coffee's journey from farm to cup.Brew: The ideal water temperature is about 90 to 96 degrees Celsius. Boiling water extracts more bitter flavours.
Coffee's journey from farm to cup.Sip: Finns drink more coffee per person than any other nation, around four cups a day.

Toys and games by size.LEGO minifigure: The minifigure's design has changed little since its 1978 debut, and billions have been made. Its C-shaped hand grips tiny accessories.
Toys and games by size.Rubik's Cube: Hungarian professor Ernő Rubik invented it in 1974 as a teaching aid. It has over 43 quintillion possible arrangements.
Toys and games by size.Hot Wheels car: Mattel's Hot Wheels began in 1968 with 16 cars and the idea of fast, flashy designs. A rare prototype pink VW bus is worth a fortune.
Toys and games by size.Classic Star Wars figure: Kenner's 3.75-inch figures launched in 1978, when Star Wars was a hit. Kids first got an Early Bird mail-in certificate, not toys, for Christmas.
Toys and games by size.Original Game Boy: The Game Boy came bundled with Tetris, and it ran for hours on four AA batteries. Its grey screen was no match for colour rivals but it won anyway.
Toys and games by size.Barbie doll: Barbie was named for Ruth Handler's daughter Barbara, and debuted in 1959. At this scale she stands 11.5 inches tall.
Toys and games by size.American Girl doll: These 18-inch dolls come with books on American history. Pleasant Rowland created the line in 1986.
Toys and games by size.Monopoly board: The game began as The Landlord's Game, created by Elizabeth Magie in 1904 to critique landlords. Parker Brothers later bought Charles Darrow's version.
Toys and games by size.Skateboard deck: Skateboards began with California surfers who wanted to "surf" on pavement when waves were flat. Early ones were wooden boards with roller-skate wheels.
Toys and games by size.Ping pong table: Ping pong began as a Victorian after-dinner game with books for a net. Official tables are 2.74 metres long.

Making chocolate, from bean to bar.Harvest the cacao pods: Cacao pods grow straight out of the tree trunk and are cut by hand with machetes; each holds dozens of beans in sweet white pulp.
Making chocolate, from bean to bar.Ferment the beans: Beans are piled under banana leaves for several days; heat from fermenting creates chocolate's flavor precursors.
Making chocolate, from bean to bar.Dry the beans: Beans are spread in the sun for about a week, which cuts moisture so they can be shipped and stored without molding.
Making chocolate, from bean to bar.Roast: Heat sets off Maillard reactions, as with coffee, giving the beans their familiar chocolatey aroma.
Making chocolate, from bean to bar.Winnow away the shells: Roasted beans are cracked and the husks blown away, leaving nibs; the shells often end up as garden mulch.
Making chocolate, from bean to bar.Grind into liquor: Grinding the nibs melts their cocoa butter into a thick liquid, called liquor, although it holds no alcohol.
Making chocolate, from bean to bar.Conch: Rodolphe Lindt invented the conche in 1879; hours of stirring make chocolate silky, and its name comes from a shell shape.
Making chocolate, from bean to bar.Temper: Controlled heating and cooling forms stable cocoa butter crystals, giving shine and snap; untempered chocolate turns dull and streaky.
Making chocolate, from bean to bar.Pour into molds: Tapping the molds shakes out air bubbles, so bars set solid and glossy.
Making chocolate, from bean to bar.Wrap: Foil protects the bar from light, heat and odors, since chocolate readily absorbs smells from nearby foods.

Movies that pushed computer graphics.Westworld: The first feature film to use computer-processed digital imagery, shown as the gunslinger robot's pixelated vision.
Movies that pushed computer graphics.Tron: It used around 15 to 20 minutes of computer graphics, and was barred from the effects Oscar because computers were deemed cheating.
Movies that pushed computer graphics.The Abyss: ILM's water pseudopod was among the first fully digital 3D creatures, convincingly mimicking moving water.
Movies that pushed computer graphics.Terminator 2: The liquid-metal T-1000 turned computer morphing into a blockbuster spectacle.
Movies that pushed computer graphics.Jurassic Park: Its dinosaurs were mostly animatronics with about six minutes of CGI; Spielberg dropped stop-motion after ILM's tests.
Movies that pushed computer graphics.Toy Story: Pixar's first feature, and the first fully computer-animated one, took four years to make.
Movies that pushed computer graphics.The Matrix: 'Bullet time' used a ring of still cameras and digital interpolation to freeze a moment while the view swirled.
Movies that pushed computer graphics.LOTR: The Two Towers: Gollum was performed by Andy Serkis in motion capture, a groundbreaking method for a lead character.
Movies that pushed computer graphics.Avatar: Cameron created a virtual camera and facial-capture rigs, and it became the highest-grossing film in history at the time.
Movies that pushed computer graphics.The Irishman: Netflix de-aged its stars with software instead of makeup or younger look-alikes.

Islands of the British Isles by area.Jersey: A Crown Dependency, not part of the UK, with its own laws and a famous breed of cow.
Islands of the British Isles by area.Isle of Wight: Home to the Isle of Wight Festival and famous for dinosaur fossils on its beaches.
Islands of the British Isles by area.Isle of Man: Hosts the Tourist Trophy motorcycle races, and its Manx cats are famously tailless.
Islands of the British Isles by area.Anglesey: Wales's largest island, and home to the village with the longest place name in Britain.
Islands of the British Isles by area.Mull: Tobermory's colorful waterfront inspired the children's TV show Balamory.
Islands of the British Isles by area.Mainland, Shetland: Home to the capital Lerwick, and the original home of the small, hardy Shetland pony.
Islands of the British Isles by area.Skye: Known for the jagged Cuillin mountains and the Fairy Pools.
Islands of the British Isles by area.Lewis and Harris: One island with two names, Lewis in the north and Harris in the south; Harris Tweed comes from the Outer Hebrides.
Islands of the British Isles by area.Ireland: The third largest island in Europe, after Great Britain and Iceland.
Islands of the British Isles by area.Great Britain: The largest island in Europe and ninth largest in the world.

Disney's Mulan, in story order.The Huns breach the Great Wall: The Ballad of Mulan dates from around the 5th century, and the legend is much older than Disney.
Disney's Mulan, in story order.Mulan's matchmaker disaster: Matchmakers were real, and the scene shows how marriage was arranged in imperial China.
Disney's Mulan, in story order.Mulan cuts her hair: In the ballad Mulan fights for twelve years, and cutting her hair marks her stepping into the army.
Disney's Mulan, in story order.Mushu joins her: Mushu is voiced by Eddie Murphy, and his character was invented for the film.
Disney's Mulan, in story order.\"I'll Make a Man Out of You\": I'll Make a Man Out of You is sung for Shang by Donny Osmond.
Disney's Mulan, in story order.An avalanche buries the Huns: The real Xiongnu nomads raided northern China, which pushed the construction of the Great Wall.
Disney's Mulan, in story order.Her secret is discovered: In the legend she is never exposed during the war; the film's discovery is a Disney addition.
Disney's Mulan, in story order.Shan Yu attacks the palace: The Imperial City scenes draw on the Forbidden City in Beijing.
Disney's Mulan, in story order.Fireworks finish Shan Yu: Fireworks were invented in China around the 9th century.
Disney's Mulan, in story order.The Emperor bows to Mulan: The film's final joke, that you don't meet a girl like that every dynasty, is among its best known.

Calendar and clock reforms.Julian calendar: Julius Caesar introduced it with leap years, advised by astronomer Sosigenes; the year of confusion before it had 445 days.
Calendar and clock reforms.Gregorian calendar: Pope Gregory XIII dropped ten days, so October 4 was followed by October 15.
Calendar and clock reforms.Scotland starts year on Jan 1: Previously the Scottish year began on March 25, but from 1600 it began on January 1.
Calendar and clock reforms.Britain adopts Gregorian: Eleven days were skipped, so September 2 was followed by September 14, and legend says people demanded their days back.
Calendar and clock reforms.French Republican calendar: It had ten-day weeks and decimal time, and lasted about twelve years until Napoleon abolished it.
Calendar and clock reforms.Japan adopts Gregorian: Japan switched in the Meiji era, and the new year moved from the lunar calendar.
Calendar and clock reforms.Greenwich Meridian chosen: An international conference in Washington picked it as the prime meridian, with France abstaining.
Calendar and clock reforms.Soviet Russia switches: A decree made 31 January followed by 14 February, so the October Revolution happened in November.
Calendar and clock reforms.Greece switches: The last European country to switch, long after the rest of Europe.
Calendar and clock reforms.Turkey switches: Ataturk's reforms also brought clocks and a new Latin alphabet in 1928.

Units of time, in seconds.Minute: The word comes from the Latin for 'small part', as in the first small division of an hour; the second is the 'second small division'.
Units of time, in seconds.Hour: Ancient Egyptians divided the day into twelve hours of daylight, and our 24-hour day may come from that tradition.
Units of time, in seconds.Day: Earth's rotation is irregular, so it gradually slows, and the length of a day is increasing by about two milliseconds each century.
Units of time, in seconds.Week: The seven-day week has no astronomical basis, and was probably spread by Babylonians and later by Jewish and Roman traditions.
Units of time, in seconds.Fortnight: This word comes from the Old English for 'fourteen nights', and it's common in British English but rare in America.
Units of time, in seconds.30-day month: Months are loosely based on the Moon's cycle, but the lunar cycle is about 29.5 days.
Units of time, in seconds.Common year: 365 days is slightly short of Earth's true orbit, about 365.2422 days, which is why leap years are needed.
Units of time, in seconds.Leap year: Years divisible by 100 are skipped unless also by 400, so 1900 wasn't a leap year but 2000 was.
Units of time, in seconds.Four-year cycle: Three common years plus one leap year gives 1,461 days, the rhythm the Julian calendar adopted under Julius Caesar.
Units of time, in seconds.Ten common years: Ten years of 365 days lasts exactly 3,650 days, but real decades usually contain two or three extra leap days.
